cards.title: Introduction to Microservices Architecture
cards.content:
What are Microservices?

Microservices architecture structures an application as a collection of small, autonomous services modeled around a business domain.

  • Independently Deployable: Services can be updated without redeploying the whole system.
  • Loosely Coupled: Services communicate via well-defined APIs (REST, gRPC, or Messaging).
  • Tech Diversity: Individual services can use different technology stacks if needed.

cards.title: Monolith vs Microservices in Spring Boot
cards.content:
Monolith vs. Microservices

In a monolithic Spring Boot app, all components (Auth, Orders, Products) reside in a single deployable JAR file.

In a microservices approach, each service is a distinct Spring Boot application with its own database schema:

// Order Service Application
@SpringBootApplication
public class OrderServiceApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(OrderServiceApplication.class, args);
    }
}

options.text: All microservices must share a single monolithic database.
Microservices should be independently deployable and loosely coupled.
Microservices require all services to be written in the exact same programming language.
Microservices communicate only via shared local file systems.

cards.title: Service Discovery with Spring Cloud Eureka
cards.content:
Why Service Discovery?

In cloud environments, microservice instances change IP addresses dynamically. A Service Registry acts as a phonebook for services.

Spring Cloud Eureka Server provides service registration and discovery:

@SpringBootApplication
@EnableEurekaServer
public class DiscoveryServerApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(DiscoveryServerApplication.class, args);
    }
}

content.text: To turn a Spring Boot application into a service discovery registry, annotate the main class with @Enable________Server.

cards.title: API Gateway with Spring Cloud Gateway
cards.content:
Role of an API Gateway

An API Gateway serves as the single entry point for external client requests, providing routing, cross-cutting concerns (authentication, rate limiting), and security.

Configuration snippet in application.yml:

spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: order-service
          uri: lb://ORDER-SERVICE
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/orders/**

cards.title: Order of API Gateway Request Processing

items.text: Client sends an HTTP request to the Gateway.
Gateway matches Predicates to determine the target route.
Gateway forwards request to downstream Microservice.
Gateway executes Post-Filters and returns response to Client.

cards.title: Resiliency with Resilience4j
cards.content:
Circuit Breakers

Distributed systems experience network delays or service failures. The Circuit Breaker pattern prevents cascading failures across microservices.

@Service
public class InventoryClient {

    @CircuitBreaker(name = "inventoryService", fallbackMethod = "getDefaultInventory")
    public InventoryStatus checkStock(String productId) {
        // Call remote Inventory Microservice
    }

    public InventoryStatus getDefaultInventory(String productId, Exception e) {
        return new InventoryStatus(productId, false); // Fallback response
    }
}

cards.title: Distributed Tracing with Micrometer and Zipkin
cards.content:
Tracing Across Services

In a microservices architecture, a single user action may traverse multiple network calls across various services.

  • Trace ID: Unique identifier assigned to an entire user request flow.
  • Span ID: Identifier for a specific segment/operation within a request flow.
  • Zipkin: Visualizes call graphs and timing details for requests.

options.text: CLOSED state stops all incoming requests immediately.
OPEN state routes all requests directly to the fallback method without invoking the remote service.
HALF_OPEN state disables fallback logic permanently.
OPEN state forces the server to restart automatically.
